claims.text: Temperature-induced surface compositional segregation governs the onset and progression of the phase transition in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are uniform and crystalline.
At room temperature, the nanoparticles are compositionally homogeneous and have no surface segregation or disorder.
The proposed test heats the nanoparticles through the premelting and melting regime under an inert atmosphere.
The controlled comparison holds particle size distribution and heating rate constant and compares particles with minor surface modifications.
Increasing temperature raises the mobility of atoms at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface atoms segregate according to differences in elemental melting points and atomic interactions.
Elements with lower individual melting points preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface compositional segregation reduces the local melting temperature.
The reduced local melting temperature triggers a disordered, amorphous-like surface layer.
The disordered surface layer progressively destabilizes the crystalline core.
With further heating, the disordered layer grows inward and ultimately produces complete particle melting.
Premelting begins at the surface at a temperature below the bulk melting point.
The appearance of the disordered surface layer will coincide with detectable surface compositional gradients.
Smaller FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles will have a larger depression of the melting-onset temperature.
Oxidation, reactive atmospheres, passivation, or substantial surface coatings may alter the proposed segregation and premelting behavior.
